3. The SystemHost¶
In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.
A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root:
```
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host
```
The noun is sys, not int, because a SystemHost is not an integration: it has no pipeline, no
app id, no blueprint parameters. The name derivation is the one you already know: OrderFlow
kebab-cases to order-flow, the system's name.
The command reads before it writes. Each scaffold in chapters 1 and 2 left a record of what it
declared — its blueprint kind and the topic you passed with -s topic=orders, in
.intropy/scaffold.json — and sys create scans the workspace for those records and assembles
them into a typed declaration:
```
system-host/
├── OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj   # .NET Aspire AppHost project
├── Program.cs                    # one entry point, two backends — you don't edit this file
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs            # the system definition, assembled from the scaffold records
├── Topics.cs                     # the system's topics, as typed refs
├── Order.cs                      # the contract type the orders topic carries
├── Properties/
│   └── launchSettings.json       # dashboard and OTLP ports
└── Taskfile.yml                  # task run → dotnet run
```
One thing is conspicuously absent: a dapr-components/ directory. The system's components are not
files anyone maintains — they are generated from the declaration you are about to read. Chapter 4
watches that happen.
One entry point, two backends¶
system-host/Program.cs
```
using System.Reflection;
using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
```
Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
that truth lives.
The declaration¶
Open Topics.cs. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:
system-host/Topics.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
public static class Topics
{
    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}
```
OrderFlowSystem.cs is the topology itself:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";
    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
    }
}
```
Nothing in these files is new information. AddExtractor and AddLoader name the blueprints you
scaffolded; "pubsub" and "orders" are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
What sys create did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.
Three things about the shape:
A topic is a value, not a string typed twice: Topics.Orders is defined once — pubsub
  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
  components. There is no second copy to drift.
The edge is derived: no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
  touching Topics.Orders is the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
Block kinds surface at the host: the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
  Publishes but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
And one thing about what is not declared: a pub/sub registration. Topics.Orders names its
pubsub component, so the system already knows it needs one — Redis gets provisioned in chapter 5
because a topic exists, not because anyone asked for a broker.
Order, the type parameter, is the contract the topic carries. The scaffold generates it as a
minimal record next to Topics.cs. It documents the contract at the declaration site and gives
schema-aware tooling something to reflect on; the wiring itself only uses the names.
Declared, then enforced¶
A declaration you edit by hand needs a gate, and Build() is it: whenever the host starts, and
whenever you run check, the declaration is validated as a whole. Any breach fails before a
single process starts.
Try it. Point the loader at a topic nobody publishes — the kind of mistake that used to live until
runtime:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "oders"));
```
```
dotnet run -- check
```
```
error: The system topology is invalid (2 error(s)):
  ITP208 [Error] topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but no component subscribes to it.
  ITP209 [Error] topic 'oders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is subscribed to but no component publishes it.
```
Both halves of the broken contract surface at once: the real topic is orphaned, and the misspelled
one has no producer. Undo the edit before moving on — the loader subscribes to Topics.Orders.
How the declaration reaches the code¶
The host never rewrites your integrations. At run time, each integration binds its topic and
component names from runtime configuration: standalone, the scaffold's local files supply it;
under the SystemHost, the host generates it from this declaration and injects it. It is the same
swap you'll watch happen to the Dapr components in chapter 4 — the code is identical in both
modes, and only who supplies the configuration changes.
Info
The declaration flow is the contract: scaffolds record what they declared, sys create
assembles the records, and from then on the host's declaration is authoritative. Parts of the
runtime half are still landing in the tooling — verify the generated-config binding against
the shipped SystemHost packages before relying on it.
Check it¶
```
cd system-host
dotnet run -- check
```
```
ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).
```
check builds and validates the topology without starting anything. Its sibling prints the model
itself:
```
dotnet run -- graph
```
```
{
  "systemName": "order-flow",
  "components": [
    { "name": "order-extractor", "kind": "extractor", "publishes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] },
    { "name": "order-loader", "kind": "loader", "subscribes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] }
  ],
  "topics": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "name": "orders", "contract": "Order" }]
}
```
That JSON is the system: the same model the run backend translates into containers and sidecars in
chapter 5, and the generate backend turns into deployable artifacts. Two backends, one truth.
Recap
sys create assembled the scaffolds' records into a typed declaration: Topics.cs defines
  each topic once, OrderFlowSystem.cs wires components to it
The extractor→loader edge is derived from sharing Topics.Orders; block kinds at the host
  mirror the blueprints
Build() validates the whole declaration; dotnet run -- check runs the same gate from the
  command line
dotnet run -- graph prints the model both backends consume; nothing has run yet

===== 01-extractor =====
1. The extractor¶
In this chapter you create the system workspace, scaffold the first of its two integrations, and run it alone: a complete integration on its own isolated components, before any system exists.
Scaffold¶
Create the workspace and render the extractor blueprint into it:
```
mkdir order-flow && cd order-flow
intropy int create extractor -n OrderExtractor -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-extractor
```
order-flow/ is the system workspace: a plain directory that holds the two integrations and, from chapter 3, the SystemHost as siblings. Nothing about it is special. Each integration stays an independent project you could version, test, and deploy on its own.
Two flags deserve a closer look:
-s topic=orders: the pub/sub topic the extractor publishes to. You'll type the same value when scaffolding the loader — each scaffold declares its own half of the contract, and records it (in .intropy/scaffold.json) for the system to assemble in chapter 3.
No empty=true: unlike the transactional tutorial, you keep the blueprint's sample logic. This tutorial is about what happens between integrations, so the insides stay stock.
The scaffold looks like the transactional layout you know, with the extractor's own components:
```
order-extractor/
├── Taskfile.yml                  # task run / build / test
├── docker-compose.yml            # local observability stack — standalone runs only
├── local/
│   ├── dapr-components/
│   │   ├── poll.yaml             # cron binding — sweeps the inbound folder every 5 s
│   │   ├── inbound.yaml          # folder binding — stands in for the source system
│   │   └── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
│   └── sample-data/
│       └── sample-order.json
├── src/                          # implemented: sweep inbound, publish to topic, delete source
└── test/
```
The sample logic ships working. On every poll tick it lists the inbound folder, publishes each file's content as a message on topic orders, and deletes the source file. And unlike the transactional integration, which runs once and exits, the extractor keeps running until you stop it — that matters in chapter 5, when you'll drop files in while the whole system is live.
Check it¶
Run the extractor standalone:
```
cd order-extractor
task run
```
The task seeds sample-order.json into the inbound folder and starts the integration under Dapr, with the sidecar loading only local/dapr-components/. Within a poll tick you should see:
```
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Swept 1 file from inbound
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)
```
Stop it with Ctrl+C, then confirm the source file is gone:
```
ls local/storage/inbound/
```
The folder is empty: the extractor swept the file, published it, and cleaned up.
Where did the message go? Into the extractor's own in-memory pub/sub — and nothing subscribes there. That's the point of an isolated run: it verifies the extractor's whole job (sweep, publish, clean up) without needing a consumer to exist. Delivery to a consumer is the system's job, and that's chapter 5.
Recap
Created the order-flow workspace; integrations and the SystemHost live in it as siblings
Scaffolded order-extractor from the extractor blueprint with its sample logic intact
Standalone, the sidecar loads only local/dapr-components/: an isolated, in-memory world
The published message intentionally went nowhere — no consumer exists yet
===== 02-loader =====
2. The loader¶
In this chapter you scaffold order-loader, the consuming half of the system, and verify it the way any subscriber is verified in isolation: by publishing through its own sidecar.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root, render the loader blueprint:
```
intropy int create loader -n OrderLoader -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-loader
```
-s topic=orders is the same value you gave the extractor, and typing it twice is deliberate: each integration declares its own half of the contract and stays verifiable alone. Chapter 3 assembles the two halves into one typed declaration — and checks that they meet.
```
order-loader/
├── Taskfile.yml
├── docker-compose.yml
├── local/
│   └── dapr-components/
│       ├── pubsub.yaml           # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
│       └── destination.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the destination system
├── src/                          # implemented: subscribe to topic, deserialize, validate, load
└── test/
```
The sample logic subscribes to orders on pubsub and, for each message, deserializes the order, validates it, and writes {orderId}.json through the destination binding. Like the extractor, it runs until you stop it.
Note that pubsub.yaml here has the same component name as the extractor's — but they are not the same broker. Each in-memory pub/sub lives inside its own integration's sidecar, so two standalone runs are two separate worlds. Keep that in mind; chapter 4 turns it into the mechanism the whole system rests on.
Publish through the loader's own sidecar¶
A subscriber alone has a problem the extractor didn't: nothing publishes to it. The answer follows from where the broker lives. The in-memory pub/sub exists inside the loader's sidecar, so any publish routed through that sidecar reaches the subscription — and dapr publish --publish-app-id does exactly that.
Start the loader in one terminal:
```
cd order-loader
task run
```
Wait for the subscription to register:
```
== APP == info: OrderLoader.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)
```
Check it¶
In a second terminal, publish an order through the loader's sidecar:
```
dapr publish --publish-app-id order-loader --pubsub pubsub --topic orders \
  --data '{"orderId":"ORD-2001","customerId":"CUST-42","orderDate":"2026-07-24T09:30:00Z","lines":[{"sku":"SKU-AAA","quantity":1,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'
```
```
Event published successfully
```
The loader picks it up and writes the destination file:
```
cat local/storage/destination/ORD-2001.json
```
```
{"OrderId":"ORD-2001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T09:31:12Z","Status":"Loaded"}
```
Stop the loader with Ctrl+C.
Recap
Scaffolded order-loader: subscribes to orders on pubsub, writes each order through the destination binding
A subscriber is verified in isolation by publishing through its own sidecar — that's where its in-memory broker lives
Both integrations now work alone, each in its own isolated world; nothing connects them yet
===== 04-component-scoping =====
4. System-scoped components¶
In this chapter you learn how the same integration code loads different Dapr components depending on who starts it: its own local set when run standalone, the system's generated overlay under the SystemHost.
One file you wrote, one the host generates¶
Open the extractor's pub/sub component:
order-extractor/local/dapr-components/pubsub.yaml
```
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.in-memory
  version: v1
```
The system's counterpart is not a file you wrote. There is no dapr-components/ directory in system-host/, and chapter 3's declaration never mentioned Redis. The host derives it: Topics.Orders names a pubsub component called pubsub, so the run backend generates one, backed by Redis because that is what the local run profile provisions:
system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml (generated)
```
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: pubsub
spec:
  type: pubsub.redis
  version: v1
  metadata:
    - name: redisHost
      value: localhost:6379
```
Same metadata.name, different spec.type. That shared name is the whole mechanism: application code addresses components by name and never learns which backing is behind it. Whoever starts the sidecar decides which file the name resolves to — and on the system side that file is generated from the topology, so the model you validated in chapter 3 and the YAML the sidecar loads cannot disagree.
The overlay¶
Standalone, you've already seen the answer: task run starts the sidecar with --resources-path ./local/dapr-components, so the integration gets its isolated, in-memory world.
Under the SystemHost, the host stages an effective component set for each integration before starting its sidecar:
Generate the system's components from the topology: one Redis-backed pubsub, because Topics.Orders names it.
Copy everything from the integration's local/dapr-components/.
Overlay the generated components: a generated component with the same metadata.name replaces the local one; new names are added.
Start the sidecar with --resources-path pointing at the staged directory, under system-host/obj/dapr-components/<integration-name>/.
For the extractor that means poll.yaml and inbound.yaml pass through untouched — sweeping a local folder is the integration's own business in both modes — while the local pubsub.yaml is replaced by the generated one.
Why an overlay, rather than handing the sidecar both directories? Because Dapr refuses duplicate component names across resource paths, and the duplicate name is the mechanism. And why not have the host generate a complete set? Then the topology would have to describe every folder binding in every integration — concerns that are the integration's own business, not the system's.
The overlay has edges worth knowing: it is staged when the host starts, so changing the topology means restarting the SystemHost; it keys on metadata.name, not the filename; and a generated component applies to every integration in the system. The Redis port is pinned to 6379, so the YAML above is exactly what the sidecars load. The staged files are real YAML on disk — inspect them whenever resolution surprises you — but editing them is futile: they are regenerated from the model on every start. Change the declaration, not the artifacts.
Check it¶
Start the system for the first time:
```
cd system-host
dotnet run
```
Leave it running and, from the workspace root in a second terminal, inspect what was staged for the extractor:
```
ls system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/
```
```
inbound.yaml  poll.yaml  pubsub.yaml
```
```
grep "type:" system-host/obj/dapr-components/order-extractor/pubsub.yaml
```
```
  type: pubsub.redis
```
The two local components passed through; the pub/sub is now the system's — generated, not written. Stop the host with Ctrl+C — the next chapter runs it for real.
Recap
Component resolution is decided by whoever starts the sidecar: the local directory standalone, the staged overlay under the SystemHost
Local components pass through untouched; a generated component with the same metadata.name replaces its local counterpart
The system's components are generated from chapter 3's declaration; the staged set under obj/ is inspectable, but regenerated on every start
Code and component names are identical in both modes; only the backing changes

1. The extractor¶
In this chapter you create the system workspace, scaffold the first of its two integrations, and run it alone: a complete integration on its own isolated components, before any system exists.
Scaffold¶
Create the workspace and render the extractor blueprint into it:
```
mkdir order-flow && cd order-flow
intropy int create extractor -n OrderExtractor -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-extractor
```
order-flow/ is the system workspace: a plain directory that holds the two integrations and, from chapter 3, the SystemHost as siblings. Nothing about it is special. Each integration stays an independent project you could version, test, and deploy on its own.
Two flags deserve a closer look:
-s topic=orders: the pub/sub topic the extractor publishes to. You'll type the same value when scaffolding the loader — each scaffold declares its own half of the contract, and records it (in .intropy/scaffold.json) for the system to assemble in chapter 3.
No empty=true: unlike the transactional tutorial, you keep the blueprint's sample logic. This tutorial is about what happens between integrations, so the insides stay stock.
The render's last line reports a project you didn't ask for: created dependency Models from template shared-models. The workspace now holds two directories:
```
order-flow/
├── Models/                       # shared contract types — scaffolded once per workspace
│   ├── Models.csproj
│   ├── Order.cs                  # the order contract the extractor publishes
│   └── OrderLine.cs
└── order-extractor/
    ├── Taskfile.yml              # task run / build / test
    ├── docker-compose.yml        # local observability stack — standalone runs only
    ├── local/
    │   ├── dapr-components/
    │   │   ├── poll.yaml         # cron binding — sweeps the inbound folder every 5 s
    │   │   ├── inbound.yaml      # folder binding — stands in for the source system
    │   │   └── pubsub.yaml       # in-memory pub/sub, component name "pubsub"
    │   └── sample-data/
    │       └── sample-order.json
    ├── src/                      # implemented: sweep inbound, transform, publish
    └── test/
```
The extractor itself looks like the transactional layout you know, with its own components. Models/ is new: the extractor template declares the shared-models template as a dependency, so scaffolding the first block into a workspace also scaffolds the workspace's contract library next to it. It holds the Order record (and its OrderLine lines): the shape the extractor publishes, defined in neither block because both halves of the system need it. The extractor references it as an ordinary ProjectReference (../../Models/Models.csproj); its own source shape stays private in src/Model/In.cs, and the pipeline's transform step maps that In to the shared Order before publishing.
The sample logic ships working. On every poll tick it lists the inbound folder, publishes each file's content as an Order message on topic orders, and deletes the source file. And unlike the transactional integration, which runs once and exits, the extractor keeps running until you stop it — that matters in chapter 5, when you'll drop files in while the whole system is live.
Check it¶
Run the extractor standalone:
```
cd order-extractor
task run
```
The task seeds sample-order.json into the inbound folder and starts the integration under Dapr, with the sidecar loading only local/dapr-components/. Within a poll tick you should see:

== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Swept 1 file from inbound
== APP == info: OrderExtractor.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Published ORD-1001 to topic orders (pubsub)

ls local/storage/inbound/

Where did the message go? Into the extractor's own in-memory pub/sub — and nothing subscribes there. That's the point of an isolated run: it verifies the extractor's whole job (sweep, publish, clean up) without needing a consumer to exist. Delivery to a consumer is the system's job, and that's chapter 5.

The render also scaffolded Models/, the workspace's shared contract library — the Order record the extractor publishes lives there, not in the extractor

The published message intentionally went nowhere — no consumer exists yet

Each in-memory pub/sub lives inside its own integration's sidecar, so two standalone runs are two separate worlds. Keep that in mind; chapter 4 turns it into the mechanism the whole system rests on.
Publish through the loader's own sidecar¶
A subscriber alone has a problem the extractor didn't: nothing publishes to it. The answer follows from where the broker lives. The in-memory pub/sub exists inside the loader's sidecar, so any publish routed through that sidecar reaches the subscription — and dapr publish --publish-app-id does exactly that.
Start the loader in one terminal:
```
cd order-loader
task run
```
Wait for the subscription to register:
```
== APP == info: OrderLoader.Pipeline[0]
== APP ==       Subscribed to topic orders (pubsub)
```
Check it¶
In a second terminal, publish an order through the loader's sidecar:
```
dapr publish --publish-app-id order-loader --pubsub pubsub --topic orders \
  --data '{"orderId":"ORD-2001","customerId":"CUST-42","orderDate":"2026-07-24T09:30:00Z","lines":[{"sku":"SKU-AAA","quantity":1,"unitPrice":12.50}]}'
```
```
Event published successfully
```
The loader picks it up and writes the destination file:
```
cat local/storage/destination/ORD-2001.json
```
```
{"OrderId":"ORD-2001","CustomerId":"CUST-42","LoadedAt":"2026-07-24T09:31:12Z","Status":"Loaded"}
```
Stop the loader with Ctrl+C.
Recap
Scaffolded order-loader: subscribes to orders on pubsub, writes each order through the destination binding
The loader's render found Models/ already scaffolded and skipped it — both blocks compile against one shared Order record
A subscriber is verified in isolation by publishing through its own sidecar — that's where its in-memory broker lives
Both integrations now work alone, each in its own isolated world; nothing connects them yet
===== 03-systemhost =====
3. The SystemHost¶
In this chapter you scaffold the SystemHost and read the file it exists for: the system's topology,
declared as typed C# and validated before anything runs.
A SystemHost is a .NET Aspire AppHost with one Intropy-specific job: it holds the system's source
of truth. One class declares which integrations exist and which topics connect them; everything
else the host does — running the system locally, generating its Dapr components, validating the
composition — is a backend over that one declaration. There is nothing to install; the
orchestration, the dashboard, and the topology model arrive as NuGet packages on first restore.
Scaffold¶
From the workspace root:
```
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host
```
The noun is sys, not int, because a SystemHost is not an integration: it has no pipeline, no
app id, no blueprint parameters. The name derivation is the one you already know: OrderFlow
kebab-cases to order-flow, the system's name.
The command reads before it writes. Each scaffold in chapters 1 and 2 left a record of what it
declared — its blueprint kind and the topic you passed with -s topic=orders, in
.intropy/scaffold.json — and sys create scans the workspace for those records and assembles
them into a typed declaration. Models/ has a record too, marked as a shared library rather than
a block, so the host reads it as the contract project: referenced, never declared as a component.
```
system-host/
├── OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj   # .NET Aspire AppHost project
├── Program.cs                    # one entry point, two backends — you don't edit this file
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs            # the system definition, assembled from the scaffold records
├── Topics.cs                     # the system's topics, as typed refs
├── Properties/
│   └── launchSettings.json       # dashboard and OTLP ports
└── Taskfile.yml                  # task run → dotnet run
```
One thing is conspicuously absent: a dapr-components/ directory. The system's components are not
files anyone maintains — they are generated from the declaration you are about to read. Chapter 4
watches that happen.
One entry point, two backends¶
system-host/Program.cs
```
using System.Reflection;
using Intropy.Topology.Aspire;
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
return args is ["run", ..] or []
    ? await IntropyAspire.RunAsync(assembly, args)      // dotnet run → the system, live (chapter 5)
    : await IntropyGenerate.RunAsync(assembly, args);   // check | graph | generate → the model, inspected
```
Both branches start the same way: discover the one system definition in this assembly, build it,
validate it. Only then do they diverge — into a live run under the Aspire dashboard, or into
verbs that inspect and export the model without starting anything. F5 and a deployment manifest
are two backends of the same truth, which is why the declaration can afford to be the only place
that truth lives.
The declaration¶
Open Topics.cs. The topic you typed into two scaffolds is now a single value:
system-host/Topics.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
using Models;
/// <summary>The system's topics, each defined once and shared by every component that touches it.</summary>
public static class Topics
{
    /// <summary>Order messages flowing from the extractor to the loader.</summary>
    public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");
}
```
OrderFlowSystem.cs is the topology itself:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
using Intropy.Topology;
/// <summary>The order-flow system: what exists, and what connects it.</summary>
public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition
{
    public string SystemName => "order-flow";
    public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
        builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);
    }
}
```
Nothing in these files is new information. AddExtractor and AddLoader name the blueprints you
scaffolded; "pubsub" and "orders" are the component and topic names from chapters 1 and 2.
What sys create did is assemble your scaffold-time declarations into one place and give them a
type. From here on, this is where the topology lives: adding an integration or renaming a topic
means editing this declaration, and the rest of the chapter is about why that is safe.
Three things about the shape:
A topic is a value, not a string typed twice: Topics.Orders is defined once — pubsub
  component name, topic name, and the contract type its messages carry — and referenced by both
  components. There is no second copy to drift.
The edge is derived: no call says "the loader depends on the extractor". Both components
  touching Topics.Orders is the wiring; the dashboard edge and the startup ordering you'll see
  in chapter 5 fall out of it.
Block kinds surface at the host: the declaration rhymes with the scaffolds. An extractor can
  Publishes but has nothing to subscribe with; a loader is the reverse. Declaring an edge a Block
  cannot have is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
And one thing about what is not declared: a pub/sub registration. Topics.Orders names its
pubsub component, so the system already knows it needs one — Redis gets provisioned in chapter 5
because a topic exists, not because anyone asked for a broker.
Order, the type parameter, is the contract the topic carries: the same record from the
workspace's Models/ library that the extractor's transform step produces and the loader's
deserializer consumes. sys create recognized the library by its scaffold record and referenced
it from the host instead of generating a contract of its own, so the declaration doesn't just say
that both ends touch a topic named orders — it carries the very type both compile against. The
wiring itself only uses the names; the type documents the contract at the declaration site and
gives schema-aware tooling something to reflect on.
Declared, then enforced¶
A declaration you edit by hand needs a gate, and Build() is it: whenever the host starts, and
whenever you run check, the declaration is validated as a whole. Any breach fails before a
single process starts.
Try it. Point the loader at a topic nobody publishes — the kind of mistake that used to live until
runtime:
system-host/OrderFlowSystem.cs
```
builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);
builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "oders"));
```
```
dotnet run -- check
```
```
error: The system topology is invalid (2 error(s)):
  ITP208 [Error] topic 'orders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is published but no component subscribes to it.
  ITP209 [Error] topic 'oders' (pubsub 'pubsub'): the topic is subscribed to but no component publishes it.
```
Both halves of the broken contract surface at once: the real topic is orphaned, and the misspelled
one has no producer. Undo the edit before moving on — the loader subscribes to Topics.Orders.
How the declaration reaches the code¶
The host never rewrites your integrations. At run time, each integration binds its topic and
component names from runtime configuration: standalone, the scaffold's local files supply it;
under the SystemHost, the host generates it from this declaration and injects it. It is the same
swap you'll watch happen to the Dapr components in chapter 4 — the code is identical in both
modes, and only who supplies the configuration changes.
Info
The declaration flow is the contract: scaffolds record what they declared, sys create
assembles the records, and from then on the host's declaration is authoritative. Parts of the
runtime half are still landing in the tooling — verify the generated-config binding against
the shipped SystemHost packages before relying on it.
Check it¶
```
cd system-host
dotnet run -- check
```
```
ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).
```
check builds and validates the topology without starting anything. Its sibling prints the model
itself:
```
dotnet run -- graph
```
```
{
  "systemName": "order-flow",
  "components": [
    { "name": "order-extractor", "kind": "extractor", "publishes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] },
    { "name": "order-loader", "kind": "loader", "subscribes": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "topic": "orders" }] }
  ],
  "topics": [{ "pubsub": "pubsub", "name": "orders", "contract": "Order" }]
}
```
That JSON is the system: the same model the run backend translates into containers and sidecars in
chapter 5, and the generate backend turns into deployable artifacts. Two backends, one truth.
Recap
sys create assembled the scaffolds' records into a typed declaration: Topics.cs defines
  each topic once, typed with the shared Order record from Models/, and
  OrderFlowSystem.cs wires components to it
The extractor→loader edge is derived from sharing Topics.Orders; block kinds at the host
  mirror the blueprints
Build() validates the whole declaration; dotnet run -- check runs the same gate from the
  command line
dotnet run -- graph prints the model both backends consume; nothing has run yet

input.prompt:
Design a detailed implementation plan for a new command `intropy sys create` in the Go CLI at /Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli. Return a step-by-step plan with file paths, function signatures, and key design decisions. Read the actual files referenced below to ground your design — do not invent APIs.

## What the command does (spec = tutorial at /Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/03-systemhost.md — read it)

`intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host`, run from a workspace root that contains integration scaffolds:
1. Scans the workspace (cwd, recursive) for `.intropy/scaffold.json` records left by `intropy int create` (use existing `template.ListScaffolds` in internal/template/scaffold_list.go).
2. Classifies records: role `shared-library` (the Models/ contracts project) → referenced project, never a component; blockKind `extractor`/`loader` → components; anything else → skip with warning.
3. Renders the existing `system-host` template from the `integrio-intropy/intropy-templates` GitHub releases (same machinery as `int create`: internal/template/create.go `Create()`, github.go, render.go). The template renders with only `name` (kebab-case) and no prompting; it derives projectName/systemClass via sprig. Template source: /Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-templates/system-host/ (read template.yaml, README.md, and the skeleton).
4. Codegen overwrites two skeleton placeholder files with assembled content:
   - `Topics.cs`: one `TopicRef<Contract>` per distinct (pubsub, topic) pair, e.g. `public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");` with `using Intropy.Topology;` and `using Models;`. Topic field name = PascalCase of topic name.
   - `<SystemClass>.cs`: `public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition` with `SystemName => "order-flow"` and `Define(SystemBuilder builder)` containing `builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor").Publishes(Topics.Orders);` / `builder.AddLoader("order-loader").Subscribes(Topics.Orders);`. Component name = the `appId` value from each scaffold record.
5. Inserts a `<ProjectReference Include="../Models/Models.csproj" />` (relative path from output dir to the shared-library project, forward slashes) into the rendered `<ProjectName>.SystemHost.csproj` — the CLI inserts references, templates never hardcode them.
6. Writes the host's own scaffold record (template.WriteScaffold — happens automatically if reusing template.Create).

## Decisions already made (do not revisit)
- Contract type per topic comes from a `contract` value recorded in scaffold.json values (a companion change adds `contract: 'Order'` to extractor/loader template spec.values in the intropy-templates repo; also consider recording `pubsub: 'pubsub'` there so the pubsub component name isn't hardcoded in the CLI). sys create reads `values.contract`, `values.topic`, `values.appId` from each record.
- Prerequisite CLI change: `internal/template/scaffold.go` must gain `BlockKind`/`DataFlow` fields populated from template labels `intropy.dev/block-kind` and `intropy.dev/data-flow` (there is an existing precedent: `Role` from `intropy.dev/template-role` via roleFromLabels; writer at internal/template/create.go:116 and internal/template/dependencies.go:132). Additive fields, no schemaVersion bump.
- Records lacking blockKind (and lacking shared-library role): skip with warning. Records with blockKind other than extractor/loader: skip with warning (v1 scope).
- v1 emits only Topics.cs + system class; no Apis.cs/Connectors.cs.

## Constraints & conventions (from prior exploration — verify by reading)
- Command layout: one file per command in cmd/intropy/ (`package main`, `var xxxCmd`, init() AddCommand). New noun `sys` → cmd/intropy/sys.go + sys_create.go. Follow cmd/intropy/manifests_create.go + internal/deploy/create.go as the structural precedent (CreateOptions with Stdin/Stdout/Stderr/HTTP/UserAgent/Owner/Repo/GitHubBaseURL test seams; CreateResult with --output-json).
- Errors: usageError via newUsageErrorf (cmd/intropy/errors.go); sentinel errors + errors.Is; wrap with context; RunE never os.Exit.
- Output: results → cmd.OutOrStdout(), progress/warnings → cmd.ErrOrStderr().
- Name derivation: -n accepts PascalCase (OrderFlow) OR kebab; system name = kebab-case. sprig's kebabcase uses github.com/huandu/xstrings ToKebabCase — the Go side must match the template's `{{ .name | kebabcase }}` semantics exactly (check go.mod whether xstrings/sprig is already a dependency of the CLI). The template itself derives projectName/systemClass from the kebab name, so the CLI passes the kebab name as the `name` value. The CLI's codegen must derive the SAME systemClass (PascalCase + "System") as the template's sprig expression `{{ .name | replace "-" " " | title | replace " " "" }}` — if they disagree, two ISystemDefinition files result and discovery throws. Decide how codegen knows the file name to overwrite (recommend: compute the same derivation in Go, or read the values back from the just-written scaffold record of the host).
- ensureOutputDir refuses non-empty without --force (internal/template/create.go) — decide flag surface: -n (required), -o (default = kebab name), --version, --force, --output-json. No -s/-f/--set (template contract: only name).
- Values trap: scaffold.json values round-trip via JSON as map[string]any (numbers = float64); topic/contract/appId are strings — validate presence + type with clear errors naming the record path.
- Validation to design: zero usable components → error with guidance; duplicate component names → error; same (pubsub,topic) with conflicting contract types → error; shared-library record missing → decide (likely error since Topics.cs needs `using Models;` and the csproj reference — or generate without the using and warn? Recommend error with guidance, tutorial guarantees Models exists).
- Multiple shared-library records → decide (error or pick + warn).
- Testing patterns: internal package tests use an httptest GitHub stub (see internal/template/create_test.go newTemplateServer and internal/deploy/create_test.go newManifestsServer, buildTarGz) — the system package test needs its own stub serving a minimal system-host template tarball; scaffold fixtures via template.WriteScaffold. Cmd-level tests run rootCmd in-process (cmd/intropy/int_list_test.go). Golden-file style assertions for generated C# are fine (check if the repo uses any golden pattern).
- README.md command tree (~line 162-184) must gain the sys noun.

## Deliverable
A concrete implementation plan: ordered steps, files to create/modify with their responsibilities, key type/function signatures (SystemModel/component/topic structs, codegen approach — embedded text/template vs fmt), the csproj insertion mechanism (string insertion before </Project> vs encoding/xml — recommend one after looking at the actual rendered csproj), the exact scan/classify/validate algorithm, flag definitions, error messages worth specifying, and a test plan (which tests, what they assert). Also list the companion changes needed in the intropy-templates repo (extractor/loader spec.values contract+pubsub; removing the dead <Name>.Contracts Exists-guard from system-host csproj — note tutorial now says host references Models/ instead). Flag any risks or inconsistencies you find while reading.

# Implement `intropy sys create`

## Context

Chapter 3 of the "Compose a system" tutorial (`intropy-techdocs/docs/tutorials/system/03-systemhost.md`, served at http://127.0.0.1:8000/tutorials/system/) specifies a new command: `intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host`. Run from a workspace root, it scans for the `.intropy/scaffold.json` records that `int create` left behind (extractor/loader blocks + the shared `Models/` library), renders the existing `system-host` template (Aspire AppHost shell with compilable placeholders), and **assembles the typed system declaration**: `Topics.cs` (one `TopicRef<T>` per topic) and `<Name>System.cs` (`ISystemDefinition` wiring components via `SystemBuilder`). Edges are derived from components sharing a topic. The host references the workspace's `Models/` project for contract types — it never generates its own contract.

Everything downstream exists and is tested: the `system-host` template (`intropy-templates/system-host/`, renders with only a kebab `name`, derives `projectName`/`systemClass`/`pubsub` via sprig) and the .NET side (`SystemBuilder`, `TopicRef<T>`, `IntropyAspire.RunAsync`, `IntropyGenerate.RunAsync` in `tooling/Intropy.Topology`).

**Decisions confirmed with user:**
- Contract type per topic comes from a `contract` value recorded in scaffold.json (companion change in intropy-templates); no heuristics, no C# parsing.
- Records lacking `blockKind` are skipped with a warning telling the user to re-scaffold (no template-name fallback).
- v1 scope: extractor + loader only; other block kinds skipped with warning. No `Apis.cs`/`Connectors.cs`.
- Host references the existing shared-library project (`Models/`); the CLI inserts the `ProjectReference` (templates never hardcode cross-project refs).

## Step 0 — prerequisite: record block-kind/data-flow labels (own commit)

The templates already declare `intropy.dev/block-kind: extractor|loader` and `intropy.dev/data-flow` labels; the CLI only copies `template-role`. Docs claim otherwise — confirmed gap.

- `internal/template/scaffold.go`: add constants `TemplateBlockKindLabel`, `TemplateDataFlowLabel`, `BlockKindExtractor`, `BlockKindLoader`; add `BlockKind`/`DataFlow` string fields to `Scaffold` (json `blockKind,omitempty` / `dataFlow,omitempty` — additive, no schemaVersion bump per comment at scaffold.go:12); helpers next to `roleFromLabels` (scaffold.go:63).
- Populate at both writer sites: `internal/template/create.go:116` and `internal/template/dependencies.go:132`.
- Tests: extend scaffold-writing tests in `internal/template/create_test.go` + `dependencies_test.go` with labeled template fixtures.

## Step 1 — `internal/system` package: assemble (pure logic)

New package modeled on `internal/deploy` (thin consumer of `internal/template`).

`internal/system/model.go`: `TopicKey{Pubsub, Name}`, `Topic{TopicKey, Contract, Field}`, `Component{AppID, Kind, Topic TopicKey, Path}`, `SharedLibrary{Path, Name}`, `Model{Name, ProjectName, SystemClass, Components, Topics, Shared}`.

`internal/system/assemble.go`:
```go
func Assemble(entries []template.ScaffoldEntry, warnf func(string, ...any)) (*Model, error)
```
- Classify: role `shared-library` → contract project; role `system-host` → skip w/ warning (keeps `--force` re-runs sane); blockKind extractor/loader → component; other blockKind → skip w/ warning ("sys create assembles extractors and loaders only"); neither → skip w/ warning ("no block kind — re-scaffold with a newer release").
- Extract values via a `stringValue(entry, key)` helper with errors naming the record path and actual type (JSON round-trip makes numbers `float64`). Required: `appId`, `topic`, `contract` (missing `contract` → guidance to re-scaffold or add `"contract": "<TypeName>"` by hand). Optional `pubsub`, default `"pubsub"`.
- Validate: zero components → sentinel `ErrNoComponents` with guidance; duplicate `appId`s → error naming both dirs; same `(pubsub, topic)` with conflicting contracts → error; zero shared libraries → error (tutorial guarantees Models/ via template dependencies); >1 shared library → error (ambiguous `using` + ProjectReference); topic field-name collision after PascalCase → error.
- Topics sorted by `(Pubsub, Name)`; `Field = pascalIdent(topic)` (`"orders"`→`"Orders"`, `"order-events"`→`"OrderEvents"`).

## Step 2 — codegen: `internal/system/codegen.go`

Embedded `text/template` const strings (no sprig). Output matches tutorial: **namespace-less** files (placeholders carry `namespace {{ .projectName }}.SystemHost;`, tutorial output has none — follow the tutorial; see companion change 4).

- `writeTopicsFile(dir, m)` — overwrites `Topics.cs`: `using Intropy.Topology;` + `using <Shared.Name>;`, `public static class Topics` with one `public static readonly TopicRef<Order> Orders = TopicRef<Order>.Define("pubsub", "orders");` per topic, generic doc comment per topic.
- `writeSystemClassFile(dir, m)` — overwrites `<SystemClass>.cs`: `public sealed class OrderFlowSystem : ISystemDefinition`, `SystemName => "order-flow"`, `Define(SystemBuilder builder)` with `builder.AddExtractor("<appId>").Publishes(Topics.<Field>);` / `AddLoader(...).Subscribes(...)`.
- **Safety gate**: before writing, stat `<dir>/<SystemClass>.cs`; if the template didn't render that placeholder, fail ("template's systemClass derivation disagrees with this CLI") — prevents the two-`ISystemDefinition` discovery failure the template.yaml:30-32 comment warns about.

## Step 3 — csproj reference insertion: `internal/system/csproj.go`

`insertProjectReference(csprojPath, include string) error` — string insertion of an `ItemGroup` with `<ProjectReference Include="../Models/Models.csproj" IsAspireProjectResource="false" />` before the last `</Project>` (verified: rendered csproj is hand-formatted XML with comments; `encoding/xml` would destroy it; `IsAspireProjectResource="false"` required or Aspire treats it as a resource). Include path from `filepath.Rel(outputDir, shared.Path)` + `shared.Name + ".csproj"`, slash-separated.

## Step 4 — orchestration: `internal/system/create.go`

`CreateOptions{Name, StartDir, OutputDir, Version, Force, OutputJSON, Stdout, Stderr, HTTP, UserAgent, Owner/Repo/GitHubBaseURL}` (same test seams as `internal/deploy/create.go`). `CreateResult` mirrors `template.CreateResult` + `System` summary (components/topics/sharedLibrary — loosely mirrors `dotnet run -- graph`).

`Create(ctx, opts)` sequence (all local validation before network I/O):
1. `kebab := xstrings.ToKebabCase(opts.Name)` — exact parity with sprig's `kebabcase` (sprig v3.3.0 delegates to xstrings; `github.com/huandu/xstrings v1.5.0` already in go.mod as indirect → promote to direct). Default `OutputDir` to kebab. The template's DNS-1123 `pattern` on `name` handles remaining format validation during Resolve.
2. `template.ListScaffolds(opts.StartDir)` → warnings to Stderr → `Assemble`.
3. Compute csproj include path (fail early).
4. `template.Create(ctx, template.CreateOptions{Template: "system-host", SetValues: {"name": kebab}, NoInput: true, Force, Version, seams...})` — gives fetch/render/`ensureOutputDir --force` semantics/dependency handling/host scaffold record (role `system-host`) for free. Don't forward OutputJSON.
5. Read back `template.LoadScaffold(filepath.Join(outputDir, template.ScaffoldRelPath))` → extract derived `projectName`/`systemClass` values. **Never reimplement the sprig `title` derivation in Go** — reading back makes CLI/template divergence impossible.
6. Placeholder gate → `writeTopicsFile` → `writeSystemClassFile` → `insertProjectReference(<projectName>.SystemHost.csproj, include)`.
7. Stderr summary: `assembled system 'order-flow': 2 components, 1 topic, contracts from Models/`. Then `maybeWriteCreateResult`.

## Step 5 — command wiring: `cmd/intropy/sys.go` + `cmd/intropy/sys_create.go`

Follow `manifests.go`/`manifests_create.go` precedent. `sysCmd` ("Manage integration systems") added to root; `sys create` with `Args: cobra.NoArgs` and flags:
- `-n/--name` (required; "PascalCase or kebab-case — OrderFlow and order-flow are equivalent")
- `-o/--output` (default: kebab-cased name), `--version`, `--force`, `--output-json`
- Deliberately **no** `-s/-f/--set/--no-input` (template contract: only `name`, never prompts).
- `signal.NotifyContext` in RunE; results→stdout, progress→stderr per repo convention.

## Step 6 — docs

`README.md` command tree (~line 165): add `sys` noun between `manifests` and `skills`, plus a short "Systems (`intropy sys`)" section with the tutorial invocation.

## Companion changes — `intropy-templates` repo (separate PR, release before this is usable)

1. `extractor/template.yaml` + `loader/template.yaml` `spec.values`: add `contract: 'Order'` and `pubsub: 'pubsub'` (keeps CLI free of literals; CLI defaults cover old records for pubsub only — missing contract errors).
2. `system-host` csproj.tmpl: delete the dead `Exists`-guarded `<Name>.Contracts` ItemGroup (tutorial now references Models/, CLI inserts it).
3. `system-host/README.md` + template.yaml description: codegen owns `Topics.cs` + `<SystemClass>.cs` and inserts the shared-library reference — not a "sibling Contracts project", not Apis/Connectors (deferred).
4. Placeholder `.cs.tmpl` files: drop `namespace {{ .projectName }}.SystemHost;` and the "Contracts project" comment so placeholder→assembled diffs are minimal (tutorial output is namespace-less).

## Tests

- `internal/system/assemble_test.go` (pure): happy path (extractor+loader+Models → 2 components, 1 deduped topic), distinct pubsubs, error table (no components / missing contract / float64 topic / dup appId / contract conflict / 0 and 2 shared libs / field collision), warning table (no blockKind, unsupported kind, system-host role), `pascalIdent` table, and a kebab-parity test asserting `xstrings.ToKebabCase` == sprig `kebabcase` rendering for sample names.
- `internal/system/create_test.go`: httptest GitHub stub (pattern: `internal/deploy/create_test.go` `newManifestsServer` + `buildTarGz`) serving a minimal-but-faithful system-host tarball; workspace fixtures via `template.WriteScaffold`. Assert exact `Topics.cs` / `OrderFlowSystem.cs` contents (inline expected strings — repo has no golden-file convention), csproj gains the Models reference before `</Project>`, host scaffold record written, `--output-json -` parses, default output dir = `order-flow`, non-empty dir without `--force` errors, validation errors occur before any HTTP request, systemClass-mismatch gate fires.
- `cmd/intropy/sys_create_test.go`: in-process rootCmd — missing `-n` → exit code 2; `--set` → unknown flag.

## Verification

1. `make check` (fmt + vet + test).
2. End-to-end against the real templates repo (after companion changes merge; before that, use `--version` pointing at a test release or run the internal tests only): replay the tutorial —
   `mkdir order-flow && cd order-flow` → `int create extractor -n OrderExtractor -s organization=Fluxia -s topic=orders -o order-extractor` → same for loader → `intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host` → inspect `Topics.cs`, `OrderFlowSystem.cs`, csproj → `cd system-host && dotnet run -- check` prints `ok: 'order-flow' is valid (2 components).` and `dotnet run -- graph` matches the tutorial JSON.

## Known gaps / follow-ups (not in this change)

- Workspaces scaffolded with older CLI builds have no `blockKind` → everything skipped, `ErrNoComponents`; the warning text is the mitigation. Worth a line in the tutorial's info box.
- Renaming the contract type in Models/ later leaves a stale `contract` value; the host's `dotnet run -- check`/compile catches it.
- `reference/cli/sys-create.md` docs page in intropy-techdocs doesn't exist yet (`docs/llms.txt` already advertises the command).
- Tutorial's `Topics.cs` shows hand-written prose doc comments; codegen emits deterministic generic ones — align the tutorial listing when this lands.

# Go CLI Best Practices

Use Cobra + Viper as the default stack for Go CLI applications. Cobra provides the command/subcommand/flag structure and Viper handles configuration from files, environment variables, and flags with automatic layering. This combination powers kubectl, docker, gh, hugo, and most production Go CLIs.

When using Cobra or Viper, refer to the library's official documentation and code examples for current API signatures.

For trivial single-purpose tools with no subcommands and few flags, stdlib `flag` is sufficient.

## Quick Reference

| Concern             | Package / Tool                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Commands & flags    | `github.com/spf13/cobra`             |
| Configuration       | `github.com/spf13/viper`             |
| Flag parsing        | `github.com/spf13/pflag` (via Cobra) |
| Colored output      | `github.com/fatih/color`             |
| Table output        | `github.com/olekukonko/tablewriter`  |
| Interactive prompts | `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea` |
| Version injection   | `go build -ldflags`                  |
| Distribution        | `goreleaser`                         |

## Project Structure

Organize CLI commands in `cmd/myapp/` with one file per command. Keep `main.go` minimal — it only calls `Execute()`.

```
myapp/
├── cmd/
│   └── myapp/
│       ├── main.go              # package main, only calls Execute()
│       ├── root.go              # Root command + Viper init
│       ├── serve.go             # "serve" subcommand
│       ├── migrate.go           # "migrate" subcommand
│       └── version.go           # "version" subcommand
├── go.mod
└── go.sum
```

`main.go` should be minimal — see [assets/examples/main.go](assets/examples/main.go).

## Root Command Setup

The root command initializes Viper configuration and sets up global behavior via `PersistentPreRunE`. See [assets/examples/root.go](assets/examples/root.go).

Key points:

- `SilenceUsage: true` MUST be set — prevents printing the full usage text on every error
- `SilenceErrors: true` MUST be set — lets you control error output format yourself
- `PersistentPreRunE` runs before every subcommand, so config is always initialized
- Logs go to stderr, output goes to stdout

## Subcommands

Add subcommands by creating separate files in `cmd/myapp/` and registering them in `init()`. See [assets/examples/serve.go](assets/examples/serve.go) for a complete subcommand example including command groups.

## Flags

See [assets/examples/flags.go](assets/examples/flags.go) for all flag patterns:

### Persistent vs Local

- **Persistent** flags are inherited by all subcommands (e.g., `--config`)
- **Local** flags only apply to the command they're defined on (e.g., `--port`)

### Required Flags

Use `MarkFlagRequired`, `MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive`, and `MarkFlagsOneRequired` for flag constraints.

### Flag Validation with RegisterFlagCompletionFunc

Provide completion suggestions for flag values.

### Always Bind Flags to Viper

This ensures `viper.GetInt("port")` returns the flag value, env var `MYAPP_PORT`, or config file value — whichever has highest precedence.

## Argument Validation

Cobra provides built-in validators for positional arguments. See [assets/examples/args.go](assets/examples/args.go) for both built-in and custom validation examples.

| Validator                   | Description                          |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `cobra.NoArgs`              | Fails if any args provided           |
| `cobra.ExactArgs(n)`        | Requires exactly n args              |
| `cobra.MinimumNArgs(n)`     | Requires at least n args             |
| `cobra.MaximumNArgs(n)`     | Allows at most n args                |
| `cobra.RangeArgs(min, max)` | Requires between min and max         |
| `cobra.ExactValidArgs(n)`   | Exactly n args, must be in ValidArgs |

## Configuration with Viper

Viper resolves configuration values in this order (highest to lowest precedence):

1. **CLI flags** (explicit user input)
2. **Environment variables** (deployment config)
3. **Config file** (persistent settings)
4. **Defaults** (set in code)

See [assets/examples/config.go](assets/examples/config.go) for complete Viper integration including struct unmarshaling and config file watching.

### Example Config File (.myapp.yaml)

```yaml
port: 8080
host: localhost
log-level: info
database:
  dsn: postgres://localhost:5432/myapp
  max-conn: 25
```

With the setup above, these are all equivalent:

- Flag: `--port 9090`
- Env var: `MYAPP_PORT=9090`
- Config file: `port: 9090`

## Version and Build Info

Version SHOULD be embedded at compile time using `ldflags`. See [assets/examples/version.go](assets/examples/version.go) for the version command and build instructions.

## Exit Codes

Exit codes MUST follow Unix conventions:

| Code  | Meaning           | When to Use                               |
| ----- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| 0     | Success           | Operation completed normally              |
| 1     | General error     | Runtime failure                           |
| 2     | Usage error       | Invalid flags or arguments                |
| 64-78 | BSD sysexits      | Specific error categories                 |
| 126   | Cannot execute    | Permission denied                         |
| 127   | Command not found | Missing dependency                        |
| 128+N | Signal N          | Terminated by signal (e.g., 130 = SIGINT) |

See [assets/examples/exit_codes.go](assets/examples/exit_codes.go) for a pattern mapping errors to exit codes.

## I/O Patterns

See [assets/examples/output.go](assets/examples/output.go) for all I/O patterns:

- **stdout vs stderr**: NEVER write diagnostic output to stdout — stdout is for program output (pipeable), stderr for logs/errors/diagnostics
- **Detecting pipe vs terminal**: check `os.ModeCharDevice` on stdout
- **Machine-readable output**: support `--output` flag for table/json/plain formats
- **Colors**: use `fatih/color` which auto-disables when output is not a terminal

## Signal Handling

Signal handling MUST use `signal.NotifyContext` to propagate cancellation through context. See [assets/examples/signal.go](assets/examples/signal.go) for graceful HTTP server shutdown.

## Shell Completions

Cobra generates completions for bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell automatically. See [assets/examples/completion.go](assets/examples/completion.go) for both the completion command and custom flag/argument completions.

## Testing CLI Commands

Test commands by executing them programmatically and capturing output. See [assets/examples/cli_test.go](assets/examples/cli_test.go).

Use `cmd.OutOrStdout()` and `cmd.ErrOrStderr()` in commands (instead of `os.Stdout` / `os.Stderr`) so output can be captured in tests.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Writing to `os.Stdout` directly | Tests can't capture output. Use `cmd.OutOrStdout()` which tests can redirect to a buffer |
| Calling `os.Exit()` inside `RunE` | Cobra's error handling, deferred functions, and cleanup code never run. Return an error, let `main()` decide |
| Not binding flags to Viper | Flags won't be configurable via env/config. Call `viper.BindPFlag` for every configurable flag |
| Missing `viper.SetEnvPrefix` | `PORT` collides with other tools. Use a prefix (`MYAPP_PORT`) to namespace env vars |
| Logging to stdout | Unix pipes chain stdout — logs corrupt the data stream for the next program. Logs go to stderr |
| Printing usage on every error | Full help text on every error is noise. Set `SilenceUsage: true`, save full usage for `--help` |
| Config file required | Users without a config file get a crash. Ignore `viper.ConfigFileNotFoundError` — config should be optional |
| Not using `PersistentPreRunE` | Config initialization must happen before any subcommand. Use root's `PersistentPreRunE` |
| Hardcoded version string | Version gets out of sync with tags. Inject via `ldflags` at build time from git tags |
| Not supporting `--output` format | Scripts can't parse human-readable output. Add JSON/table/plain for machine consumption |
